On 2023-08-30, Lizy Thomson, Nathan Seldon, Stephen Donohoe, and Clari solution engineer Curt Weaver discussed Clari’s offerings and how Nathan’s company currently forecasts and measures revenue for its Martrus payments product. Stephen Donohoe intended to follow up with options based on the company’s data and forecasting needs; no product demonstration took place in the segment provided.

Lizy Thomson asked whether Clari could provide KPI dashboards comparing sales-representative performance and rolling metrics up to sales leaders. Her company currently manages these KPIs manually in Excel using formulas and has recently converted them to Power BI. Curt Weaver said Clari could potentially support this through a separate KPI-focused dashboard or roll-up, in addition to the standard forecast view; the specific KPIs and formulas would need to be reviewed. Examples Curt mentioned included average selling price and sales-cycle length.

Clari representative Stephen Donohoe said that determining whether the company’s KPI reporting could be implemented in a dashboard would require understanding which KPIs it tracks and how those metrics are calculated and visualized in Excel and Power BI. He suggested a mutual NDA could enable the company to share those details.

Nathan Seldon described Martrus as a fintech payments product aimed at seafarers employed by shipping companies, which are the company’s target market across its products. Martrus offers crew payments, an e-wallet for seafarers, and vendor payments. The value proposition is faster payments, fewer transaction fees, and a stronger compliance platform.

Nathan Seldon said Martrus charges about $12 per crew-pay transaction, typically once per month per seafarer. Crew-payment revenue is relatively predictable if the customer provides the number of crew members and confirms monthly payment frequency. Vendor payments are also relatively predictable when the customer provides transaction volumes; Nathan cited a fee of around $15 per bank-to-bank transfer.

Nathan Seldon explained that Martrus e-wallet revenue is harder to forecast than crew and vendor payments. Seafarers choose whether to adopt the wallet and how often to send money to family, withdraw cash, or use the card; usage generates transfer fees and smaller foreign-exchange revenue. Adoption and usage are voluntary and difficult to predict, and account ramp can fall short: an account estimated at $100,000 in value might generate only $30,000 within twelve months if wallet adoption is low.

Clari representative Stephen Donohoe introduced Nathan Seldon to Johnny from compliance, a contact at an existing Clari customer. Stephen said that customer had used Clari for several years and had a similar technology stack, including Kaia and Outreach; Nathan said he would try to connect with Johnny that week.

In a discussion about Tesla’s sales in China, the speaker said Tesla had faced tariffs, shipping costs, and limited access to subsidies. The speaker expected local production, locally sourced components, and Tesla’s addition to a purchase-tax exemption to improve costs and competitiveness; parts made in China were not subject to the tariff being discussed.

The speaker explained that shipping cars from California to Europe and Asia created logistical and cash-flow challenges: Tesla could have to pay suppliers before receiving payment from customers. Local production on the same continent could reduce shipping friction and improve Tesla’s financial health. The speaker contrasted this with sales to nearby California customers, where payment could arrive before supplier bills were due, and said an asset-backed line of credit partly helped offset the cash-flow mismatch.

The speaker described shipping from the U.S. West Coast to Europe as especially difficult, involving the Panama Canal or the much longer route around Tierra del Fuego. The speaker said Panama Canal backups could cause major delays and joked about ships ending up near Antarctica.

The speaker said Tesla chose a factory site near Berlin, technically in Brandenburg and roughly 30 minutes from Berlin’s outskirts, after considering many locations and needing to move quickly. BMW had previously considered the site for a plant, so about a year’s worth of environmental paperwork and permits had already been completed. Local and state governments were supportive, and the site had access to a small train station that was to be moved so workers could get off the train near the factory.

The speaker viewed the Berlin-area factory location as a good combination: it was close enough for young employees to live in Berlin and commute, while the surrounding area offered more affordable homes with yards for families. The speaker also noted that the area had considerable talent.

When asked about Berlin’s advantages over other European locations, the speaker joked that Berlin had the best nightclubs. The conversation also jokingly entertained the idea of a nightclub at the factory.

The speaker said Tesla might add a roller-coaster-like ride at the Fremont factory, using a rail capable of carrying modified Tesla vehicles, and described the idea as potentially fun. Existing vehicle-conveyance systems in the factory were compared to slow-moving roller coasters.

The speaker said Tesla felt positive about its direction, citing the Model Y, battery announcements, Autopilot progress, the Gigafactory, new vehicle development, and efforts to roll out the solar glass roof. The speaker also said the Cybertruck had been received very well and that the number of orders exceeded expectations.

The speaker said the Cybertruck was expected to be Tesla’s best product ever and described it as an aggressive, intimidating, badass truck. The interviewer remarked that many U.S. pickup buyers want the toughest-looking truck, and compared the Cybertruck to a tank from the future.
